add_nodes.title: Satellites in orbit switch to post-quantum keys with proven update paths
add_nodes.description: At least one operator of long-lived satellites (GEO, MEO or a government constellation) switches the key exchange and command authentication of several operational satellites from RSA or elliptic-curve algorithms to post-quantum or hybrid algorithms in orbit, using rekey and update protocols with machine-checked proofs. Achieved means the operator discloses the switch and the proofs, or a government buyer confirms them.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No operational fleet has switched in orbit. NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft, Nov 2024) deprecates 112-bit RSA and ECC by 2030 and disallows quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms by 2035. CNSA 2.0 requires new national-security acquisitions to comply from Jan 1 2027 and aims for quantum-resistant national-security systems by 2035 (general). Telecommand on pre-shared AES-256 keys is already quantum-safe.
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (mandate deadlines; the AI-math share is the machine-checked update path)
add_nodes.why: The deadlines force a switch with or without AI. AI makes the switch on a 15-year asset safe to attempt: the rekey and update protocols carry machine-checked proofs, so a failed swap is unlikely to cost the command link. Only satellites that do public-key operations on board need it; bent-pipe GEO payloads and AES-only telecommand do not. Satellites launched from about 2030 with agile crypto reach their cutover windows as NIST's 2035 date and the CNSA 2.0 milestones approach. S2: architecture 2028, flight demo 2029, contracts and launches 2030-32, first disclosed fleet cutover 2033. S3 2032, because proofs are near-free from 2029. S1 2034. Disclosure is the main risk, which holds S2 at Low.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Most operators will replace satellites or rely on pre-shared symmetric keys and ground-side controls, so few in-orbit switches happen. Government programs that do switch will not disclose the details.
add_nodes.signpost: A GEO or government operator announcing a completed in-orbit post-quantum cutover with published proofs; CNSA 2.0 compliance reports for space systems.
add_nodes.note_2035: This is the 2032-35 end of the post-quantum chain, timed by NIST's 2035 cutoff and CNSA 2.0. S4 adds nothing because mandates, contract lags and operator choice bind.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: A constellation shell designed with certified tools enters service
add_nodes.description: A new constellation shell or satellite generation whose orbits, beam plan, spectrum use and laser topology came from a design optimizer with certified interference and capacity bounds (comms-constellation-design-optimizer) is built, launched and in commercial service, and its coordination showings carry those bounds. Achieved means the operator states that a shell in service was designed this way, or its filings show it.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: None. More than 10,000 commercial communications satellites operate in LEO and 50,000+ more are planned; design tools are in-house and uncertified. V3 Starlink satellites need Starship (33FG).
add_nodes.why: Design tools act through new satellites. From a filing to a shell in service takes one satellite generation plus deployment: 18-36 months in 2026, 0.5-0.7x of that by 2031, plus launching hundreds of satellites. S2: optimizer used in a filing 2029, satellites built 2030-31, service 2032. S3: 2028 and 2031. S1: 2031 and 2034. Many filings are placeholders and operators may not say how a shell was designed, which holds S2 at Medium for 2035.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Launch, manufacturing, spectrum rights and business plans shape constellations more than design software. Incumbents' in-house tools are good, and the certified bounds may change a design by a few percent.
add_nodes.signpost: An operator or new entrant stating that a shell in service came from a design optimizer with certified bounds; coordination showings for a new shell that cite certified interference bounds.
add_nodes.note_2035: Inside the 2035 horizon in S1-S4. S4 adds nothing because satellite output at the leading operators is launch-bound, which the S4 analysis shows for Starlink.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: AI-designed codes ship in satellite-to-phone standards
add_nodes.description: An AI-designed short-block code, decoder or synchronization scheme with machine-checked finite-blocklength claims is part of a published 3GPP non-terrestrial-network release or a CCSDS standard, and ships in handsets, modems or ground terminals.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No AI-designed code is in any 3GPP or CCSDS standard. LLM-guided search found seven record binary linear codes in Sep 2026 (arXiv 2609.37056). 3GPP's first normative 6G work is expected in Release 21, with commercial 6G around 2030 (general).
add_nodes.why: Short blocks are where coding gains remain, and 0.5 dB on a handset uplink at the beam edge can decide whether a link closes. Standards cycles take 2-4 years and chipsets 1-2 more, and committees do not speed up with cognition, so S3 equals S2. S2: contributions from 2028, a release freeze around 2030-31, shipping 2032. S1: 2034. Standards bodies are conservative and decoder complexity and patents decide adoption, which holds S2 at Medium.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Most links already use standardized LDPC, turbo or polar codes within tenths of a dB of finite-blocklength bounds. 6G channel coding may be fixed before AI-designed proposals are ready, leaving the next window after 2035.
add_nodes.signpost: A 3GPP or CCSDS contribution with an AI-designed code that is accepted into a release; a chipset vendor shipping it.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: standards and chipset cycles put the first shipping AI-designed codes in 2032-34. S4 adds nothing because committees and chipset cycles bind.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: Aviation approves low-orbit navigation with proven integrity
add_nodes.description: An aviation authority (FAA or EASA) or an ICAO standard accepts a LEO navigation service, alone or combined with GNSS, for an operation that needs integrity, for example through an RTCA or EUROCAE avionics standard, resting on the provider's published integrity overbounds and fault statistics.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No aviation approval of any LEO navigation service. Xona announced on Oct 7 2026 that Pulsar is entering scaled production (Xona). Aviation GNSS integrity standards such as SBAS and ARAIM took about a decade each (general).
add_nodes.why: Aviation needs integrity at about 1e-7 per approach (general), and overbounds for a new constellation need years of its own fault history. Chain (S2): service with published bounds 2029, three or more years of fault data, avionics standards drafted in parallel, approval 2035 at the earliest. S3 drafts the proofs and safety case almost for free, so the remaining time is fault data and committee calendar: 2034. Institutions set the pace and no named approval path exists for LEO navigation, so S2 stays Speculative and S3 Low.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Aviation integrity standards change over a decade. Spoofing pressure may push aviation toward hardened GNSS receivers and inertial sensors before it accepts a new satellite service.
add_nodes.signpost: An RTCA or EUROCAE working group opening a standard for LEO navigation; ICAO navigation-systems panel work on LEO signals; a provider publishing several years of fault-rate data.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. Fault-history data and aviation committees bind, so the node sits at the edge of the horizon in every scenario and S4 adds nothing.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

add_nodes.title: A deep-space ground station uses a receiver that beats photon counting
add_nodes.description: An operational optical ground station receiving from a deep-space or far-cislunar laser terminal uses a joint-detection receiver and returns more bits per received photon than optimized pulse-position modulation with photon counting, under live conditions.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: None. NASA's DSOC returned 13.6 Tbit and ended on Sep 2 2025. Joint detection has been shown only in the lab (Green Machine, 2025).
add_nodes.why: After a ground demo, a station upgrade takes about 2-3 years of engineering and funding, and it needs a laser terminal flying at deep-space range. No committed deep-space optical mission for 2032-35 is known (general), so mission availability and budgets bind. S3: demo 2030, station 2033. S2: 2031 and 2034. S1: after 2035. Background light and optical loss shrink the gain, which keeps every band at Low or below.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: PPM with superconducting detectors keeps improving and is within a few dB of practical limits (general). Agencies may prefer larger apertures, which are proven, over a new receiver.
add_nodes.signpost: NASA, ESA or JAXA funding a joint-detection receiver for an operational optical ground station; a deep-space mission with an optical terminal manifested for 2032-35.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon, extending the receiver chain to operations. S4 adds nothing because flight opportunities, budgets and background-light physics bind.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-networks (2026-10-07): horizon 2035 and S4 review. New node for the 2035 horizon.

patch.thesis: Certified routing and interference bounds put meshes and phone-to-satellite service on proven plans by 2029-30 (base case). Through 2035 the rest moves at the pace of WRC-31, NIST's 2035 crypto cutoff, standards cycles and launches. S4 adds nothing over S3, because no gate here is labor-bound.
patch.reader_hook: The FCC's 2026 rules judge satellite interference against simulated criteria, such as 3% throughput loss, which turns spectrum rights into a math problem. NIST's draft rules disallow today's public-key encryption in 2035. A GEO satellite launched in 2028 flies to about 2043. Qubit estimates for breaking RSA-2048 fell from 20 million (2019) to under 100,000 (2026).
